description: SiteLight AI is an independent team passionate about artificial intelligence, space exploration, and innovative software development. Combining expertise in full-stack development, AI agents, and 3D visualization, our goal is to develop an interactive Lunar Landing Site Navigator that enables users to explore, analyze, and compare potential Moon landing sites using NASA's scientific data, interactive simulations, and AI-powered insights.
summary: SiteLight is a web application that helps people compare lunar south-pole study sites and mission dates. It brings NASA terrain data and Sun-Earth geometry into one clear, interactive workspace. Users can compare two scenarios, see sunlight and Earth-visibility windows, inspect the local horizon, and test alternative start times within the loaded data. Terrain screening and historical thermal,Apollo seismic records add context, while clearly labeled research models explore engineering assumptions. An evidence section connects results to their sources, and downloadable reports preserve the settings and limitations. Our goal is to make complex lunar planning information easier for educators, the public and early-stage mission teams to understand. The public demo uses prepared real-data records; additional on-demand scientific calculations require the separate backend. SiteLight supports exploration and comparison, not flight certification or a guarantee of landing safety.
details:
AppLink: https://sitelight.vercel.app/  Sourcecode: https://github.com/manojkalyan/siteLight

The problem

At the lunar south pole, nearby terrain can block the Sun or Earth. A small change in location or date can change lighting and direct-to-Earth visibility. Comparing these trade-offs across separate technical tools is difficult for non-specialists.

Our solution

SiteLight places two independent mission scenarios in one visual workspace. Users select study sites, UTC start times and duration, then compare sunlight, Earth visibility and simultaneous availability against shared requirements. The app explains which conditions fall short and keeps an alternative date as a preview until the user applies it.

How it works

A Python preparation pipeline processes NASA LOLA terrain and pinned JPL/NAIF SPICE kernels. It calculates local terrain horizons and sampled Sun/Earth directions. The browser evaluates available records against user requirements and displays timelines, horizon plots and comparison results. Source manifests retain acquisition details and SHA-256 identities. Missing coverage is reported rather than filled with invented measurements.

What is creative

The main contribution is an understandable, evidence-linked comparison workflow: compare sites, identify the limiting condition, preview a different start, and inspect the source behind the result. Historical Apollo impact waveforms and moonquake/scarp context connect visible terrain with subsurface science without pretending to predict a local seismic hazard.

Benefits and intended impact

Educators and the public can understand why lunar timing matters. Early-stage mission teams can communicate site/date trade-offs and revisit assumptions when schedules change. The intended impact is clearer decisions and better scientific communication; operational time savings and mission safety improvements have not been established by field trials.

Tools and implementation

The interface uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js and Vite. The scientific preparation/service uses Python, NumPy, rasterio, SPICE/spiceypy and FastAPI. Node tests and Playwright support software checks. GitHub hosts the source and Vercel hosts the public frontend. No specialized physical hardware is required to view the prototype.

Factors considered

We considered polar terrain obstruction, solar elevation, Earth visibility, overlapping windows, data coverage, sampling intervals, uncertainty, source traceability, performance, screen size and readable explanations. The cinematic terrain is illustrative; quantitative terrain analysis uses the separately identified DEM data.

Current scope

The public frontend runs prepared real-data assessments, comparisons, loaded January-March 2027 starts, historical context, exploratory models and exports. The separate scientific backend is not connected to the public deployment. New custom terrain points, dates outside bundled coverage, monthly record generation and recomputed terrain ensembles need that backend. Results are a research prototype, not NASA approval or flight-qualified advice.
